clue.text: Extra work that’s from The Sun?

blocks.clueFragment: Extra work that’s from The Sun?
blocks.note: surface reading: a side job writing for a British tabloid newspaper
setter's reading: the glow of the moon is sunlight bounced back, so a second job is named after that borrowed light

explanation.walkthrough: The italics make The Sun the tabloid newspaper, so you picture freelance journalism; the real joke is that the moon only shines with light that comes from the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking a second job on top of your regular employment, often secretly and at night, is the familiar idiom for this.

clue.text: Male topless, doing spring cleaning

indicators.note: without a top means the word loses its uppermost letter, which in a down entry is the first

blocks.note: M is the standard abbreviation for male
to spring is to hop, so doing it is hopping

explanation.surface: A shirtless man doing the annual spring clean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring cleaning' reads as one phrase, but 'spring' belongs to the wordplay and 'cleaning' stands alone as the definition. HOPPING loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: Wiping floors with a wet sponge on a stick is a common household chore, so the verb form fits the gerund.

clue.text: OMG! Mike's dropped a clanger

indicators.note: something dropped is let fall and left behind, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: taken as written: the texting exclamation
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone gasps 'Oh my God!' because Mike has made an embarrassing blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing M from OMG leaves OG, the abbreviation used in football scores for an own goal, so the wordplay produces an abbreviation that the answer spells out in full.
explanation.definitionFit: A clanger is a British word for an embarrassing blunder, and scoring into your own net is the sporting image of one.

clue.text: Sluggish Raleigh cyclist exhausted on Tour

indicators.note: emptied out, with the inside used up, so only the two outer letters remain
touring means travelling around, so these letters wander into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A worn-out rider on a Raleigh bike crawls through the Tour de France.
explanation.walkthrough: Raleigh is a British bicycle maker, which makes the cycling picture convincing; here it is only letters to be mixed with the outside of 'cyclist'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking energy and moving slowly is the plain synonym, describing someone drowsy, listless or torpid.

clue.text: Drink Bash Street kid chucked up

indicators.note: thrown upwards, which in a down entry turns the letters to read from bottom to top

blocks.note: Plug is one of the Bash Street Kids, the schoolboy gang in the British children's comic The Beano

explanation.surface: A comic-strip schoolboy has a drink and promptly throws up.
explanation.walkthrough: You need to know that Plug, the toothy one, belongs to the Bash Street Kids in the long-running Beano comic.
explanation.definitionFit: To swallow liquid in one large mouthful is a vivid way of taking a beverage, so the verb matches.

clue.text: Waifs exposed without underwear in burlesque

indicators.note: stripped of the outer covering, so the first and last letters are peeled away
in the old sense of outside, so one piece sits around another

blocks.note: waifs are strays, and the inside of that word is kept
a vest is a British undershirt

explanation.surface: Scantily clad young things strip off their undies in a saucy cabaret show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without underwear' reads as naked, but 'without' means outside, so the vest goes inside. In Britain a vest is a sleeveless undershirt, not a waistcoat.
explanation.definitionFit: A burlesque is a grotesque parody or mockery, which is exactly what a distorted imitation of something serious is.

clue.text: Trump wants one head of BBC arrested by Christmas

definitions.note: describes the prize rather than naming it

indicators.note: the head of a word is its leading letter
someone arrested is held in custody, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: Noel is another word for Christmas
the first letter

explanation.surface: Trump wants a BBC boss locked up over Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Trump's feuds with the BBC; in fact 'Trump wants one' is the definition, pointing at the peace prize he has openly coveted.
explanation.definitionFit: Donald Trump has repeatedly and publicly said he deserves the peace prize awarded in Oslo, so this is one he wants.

clue.text: Warning: hipsters lifted by US federal agents …

indicators.note: raised upwards, which in a down entry flips the letters to read from the bottom
placed beside, so one piece sits next to the other in the column

blocks.note: the ton is an old term for fashionable society, the trendsetters
ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the American federal agency

explanation.surface: A warning that trendy young people are being picked up by US immigration officers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' looks like arrested, matching the agents, but it only turns the fashionable set upside down. The ellipsis runs the sentence on into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Advance notification that something is coming, as in giving a week's notice, is a standard synonym for a caution.

clue.text: … one after another for speaking out can be put in prison

indicators.note: speaking out means saying aloud, so what matters is how the phrase sounds

blocks.note: doing things one after another is doing them in turn

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: people who speak out, one after another, can end up behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this to the clue before, so the surface reads as a protest against detention; the wordplay is just a two-word phrase said out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: To intern is to confine someone, typically a foreign national or suspect, without trial during wartime or emergency.

clue.text: Stew over review of "beige" Hamlet?

indicators.note: to review is to look back over, so the letters are read backwards
lying over and across something covers it, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: paella is a Spanish rice dish cooked in one pan, loosely a stew
tan is a light brown shade, close to beige

explanation.surface: A theatre critic stews over a review calling a production of Shakespeare's Hamlet bland.
explanation.walkthrough: Italics make Hamlet look like the play, but Hamlet is a British brand of cigar; the question mark flags that it is an example, not a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A long thin cigar is the type, and Hamlet is a well-known brand of small cigars, so it is given by example.

clue.text: Tired old PM must change direction ...

indicators.note: turning from one direction to the other swaps right for left inside the word

blocks.note: Gordon Brown was a British Prime Minister from 2007 to 2010

explanation.surface: A weary former Prime Minister is told he must do a U-turn.
explanation.walkthrough: R (right) becomes L (left). The ellipsis carries on into the next clue to make one sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out of breath, as a horse after a hard gallop, is an older British sense of the word, meaning exhausted.

clue.text: ... line from article penned by bonkers Boris

indicators.note: bonkers means crazy, so these letters are scrambled into a mad order
something penned is shut in an enclosure, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a is the indefinite article
taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a line from a newspaper article written by a wild Boris Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: Boris Johnson was a journalist and columnist before becoming Prime Minister, which makes 'article penned by' sound like his byline; 'penned' here means enclosed.
explanation.definitionFit: On a weather chart, a curve joining places of equal atmospheric pressure is a particular kind of line.

clue.text: What will gamer do in first-person shooter Inferno?

definitions.text: What will gamer do in first-person shooter

blocks.clueFragment: What will gamer do in first-person shooter
blocks.note: first meaning, split as a short sentence: what the player will do is shoot
second meaning: the flames of the damned

explanation.surface: A question about how a player behaves in a shooting video game called Inferno.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as HE'LL FIRE: in a shooter the gamer pulls the trigger. Italics make Inferno look like the game's title, but it is the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante's poem about the underworld is called Inferno, and the burning torment of damnation is what the word names.

clue.text: S&M gear seen across naked cult's camps

indicators.note: stripped of the outer covering, so just the inner letters are kept
stretched across something means spanning it, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: gags are mouth restraints, kit used in bondage play
the inside two letters

explanation.surface: Bondage equipment is spotted at a nudist sect's encampments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Camps' sits at the end looking like part of the scene; it is the definition, with the 's attached to the cult acting as 'has' or simply joining.
explanation.definitionFit: The Soviet network of forced labour prisons gave its acronym to such places, now a general term for harsh detention compounds.

clue.text: Minister ultimately crushed by wagging tongues?

definitions.text: Minister ultimately crushed by wagging tongues?

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the closing letter is taken
something crushed is mangled out of its shape, so these letters are broken up and reformed

blocks.note: the final letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A government minister finally brought down by gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicola Sturgeon was Scotland's First Minister until 2023, resigning amid a storm of scandal and speculation; the whole clue is both her story and the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish leader who resigned in 2023 while rumours and a police inquiry swirled fits a minister brought low by gossip.

clue.text: Child's hero hurt, twice snubbed by Adult Choice

indicators.note: to be snubbed is to be cut, and twice means it happens two times, so a letter is cut out twice

blocks.note: Jack Reacher is the hero of Lee Child's thriller novels
to ache is to hurt
A is the old film certificate for adult

explanation.surface: A kid's favourite superhero is wounded and ignored twice by the grown-ups' choice award.
explanation.walkthrough: Child is the novelist Lee Child, not a youngster. Both A's go from the joined pieces, one from each.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrowed from French, the word means rare, exquisite and sought after, which is the adjectival sense of choice.

clue.text: Fiddle endlessly with once bright bloomers

indicators.note: without ends means both the opening and closing letters are cut off, keeping the inside

blocks.note: glad once meant bright or shining, an archaic sense
a fiddle is a violin, with its inside letters kept

explanation.surface: Someone keeps fussing over a pair of old, brightly coloured knickers.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloomers look like underwear, but here they are things that bloom. 'Once' marks the archaic sense, and 'with' simply puts the two pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: Tall plants with spikes of showy flowers, these are things that bloom, which is the punning sense of the word.

clue.text: Count’s about to break wind in front of Lord Lieutenant

indicators.note: placed ahead, so one piece comes before the other in the row
breaking something splits it apart so another piece can sit in the gap

blocks.note: to wind thread or yarn is to roll it up
ca is the abbreviation of circa, about
LL is the abbreviation for Lord Lieutenant

explanation.surface: An aristocrat is about to pass gas in front of the monarch's county representative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like a nobleman and 'break wind' like flatulence; both are split. A Lord Lieutenant is the British monarch's representative in a county.
explanation.definitionFit: Reading out a list of names to check who is present is a way of counting heads, so the noun fits.

clue.text: Brother inspired by Mick Hucknall album?

indicators.note: to be inspired is to have something breathed into you, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: Mick Hucknall, flame-haired singer of Simply Red, is widely known as Red
'Brother!' and 'Cor!' are both exclamations of surprise

explanation.surface: Was a sibling the inspiration behind a Mick Hucknall album?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brother' looks like a relative but is an exclamation; cor is British slang for surprise, as in 'cor blimey'.
explanation.definitionFit: A disc of music released by an artist is commonly called this, the older name for an LP or album.

clue.text: Make pass after getting round in bar

indicators.note: getting something means taking it in, so one piece is received inside the other

blocks.note: in fencing a lunge is a thrust or pass at the opponent
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Someone makes a pass at a person after buying a round of drinks in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The pub scene of a round and a pass is a red herring. A lounge is the more comfortable room of a British pub, the lounge bar.
explanation.definitionFit: In British pubs the lounge bar is the smarter room, so the shortened name is a kind of bar.

clue.text: Firm training received by Himmler's baby spies

indicators.note: something received is taken in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the SS was the Nazi paramilitary force that Himmler led
Co is the abbreviation for company
PE is physical education

explanation.surface: Spies receive tough training from the Nazi police chief's pet organisation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm training' reads as rigorous drill, but firm is a business and training is school sport.
explanation.definitionFit: To scope something out is informal for to examine or survey it, so the verb sense matches spying.

clue.text: Music producer in shot: “Cut!”

indicators.note: a cut shortens, so the final letter is trimmed away

blocks.note: a shot is a photo, informally a pic
the punctuation mark in the clue is itself named

explanation.surface: A film director shouts 'Cut!' while a record producer is in the shot.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon is not punctuation but part of the wordplay: name it and lose its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A small high-pitched flute makes music, so calling the instrument something that produces music is a witty disguise.

clue.text: Cunning mum ruined late husband

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked and broken up, so these letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: mum means silent, and 'st!' is a call for silence
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A scheming mother destroyed her dead husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' is not a mother: it means keep quiet, and ST is an old hushing sound like 'psst'.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting secretly and slyly to avoid notice is a sense close to craftiness, the noun of guile.

clue.text: Bats flap over water

indicators.note: turned over, so the letters are flipped round to read right to left

blocks.note: bats are clubs used to hit a ball
a flap is a fuss, as is ado

explanation.surface: Bats flutter their wings above a river or lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' and 'flap' paint flying animals; they are sporting clubs and a panic.
explanation.definitionFit: Carbonated mixer water is sold under this name, so it is a specific kind of water.

clue.text: On reflection, is the First Lady a riddle?

indicators.note: a mirror reflection shows things back to front, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: taken as written
in the Bible Eve was the first woman

explanation.surface: A thoughtful question: is the US President's wife something of an enigma?
explanation.walkthrough: First Lady suggests the White House, but the first lady of all is Eve. A riddle is also a coarse garden sieve.
explanation.definitionFit: A riddle in its older sense is a large coarse mesh used for sifting soil or gravel, a kind of strainer.

clue.text: Deliver prompt following short pause

indicators.note: falling short means coming up one letter shy, so the final one goes
coming after, so one piece is placed behind the other

blocks.note: a rest is a pause, in music especially
a cue is a prompt to an actor

explanation.surface: Instructions to hand over a prompt after a brief break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliver prompt' reads as 'deliver promptly'; prompt is a noun here, and deliver means to save.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliver someone from danger is to save them, the same as the verb meaning to free or recover.

clue.text: Virtually immaculate conception

indicators.note: virtually means almost but not quite, so the word stops one letter short

blocks.note: ideal means perfect, flawless

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase looks like the Immaculate Conception of Christian doctrine; 'conception' is the definition, in the sense of a notion.
explanation.definitionFit: A conception can be a mental notion or thought, so it is a straight synonym in the abstract sense.

clue.text: Rat run sent back through Parisian thoroughfare

indicators.note: returned to where it came from, so the letters are read backwards
passing through something means being inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: rue is French for a street
to run is to go, as an engine does

explanation.surface: A rodent's route is diverted back through a street in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rat run' reads as one phrase, a British term for a side-street short cut, but 'Rat' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a dishonest, unprincipled person, a scoundrel who cannot be trusted.

clue.text: Traditional style sold in fashion houses close to Edinburgh

indicators.note: done in a new fashion, so these letters are reshaped
the close of a word is its end, so its final letter is taken
to house is to give shelter, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
cool as a noun is fashionable style or panache
the final letter

explanation.surface: Classic designs are on sale in the couture houses near Edinburgh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Traditional style' wants to be the definition, but style supplies letters. 'Fashion houses' looks like a couture label; the words belong to different devices.
explanation.definitionFit: Describing conservative, old-fashioned ways and values, the hyphenated adjective is a near synonym of conventional or customary.

clue.text: Kamala Harris, originally filling for Joe Biden, came unstuck as leader

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so opening letters are taken
a filling is what sits in the middle, so the centre letter is kept
coming unstuck means falling apart, so these letters are reassembled differently

blocks.note: the initials of the two names
the central letter
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Kamala Harris, stepping in for Joe Biden, came apart as the Democrats' figurehead.
explanation.walkthrough: The US election story is a decoy: the answer is the British politician who became Leader of the Conservative Party in 2024.
explanation.definitionFit: She was elected head of the UK Conservative Party and Leader of the Opposition in November 2024, so she is a party chief.
